articles.title: Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach
articles.summary: The US military said a vessel trying to leave an Iranian port was hit due to the naval blockade on the country. On its part, Iran said three "non compliant" oil tankers caught fire in the Strait of…

image.caption: The US has been blocking vessels trying to use Iranian ports for months as it tries to push Iran to lift its own blockade [FILE: October 2026]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: The United States struck a commercial ship attempting to breach its naval blockade on Iran, the US military said Sunday.

According to the US Central Command (CENTCOM), the cargo vessel "tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," before its stern was struck by "precision munitions" shot from a US military aircraft.
In a video posted by CENTCOM, an explosion can be seen on the M/V Huda's stern as a result of the shooting, with the ship's civilian crew ignoring "repeated warnings."
The authorities in the UAE said 22 people had been rescued due to a fire on a vessel in the Gulf of Oman.
What's the situation in the Strait of Hormuz?
The US naval blockade on Iran, intended to pressure the country into lifting its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, has been in force for months.
Iran's own blockade of the waterway, through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas supplies flowed before the war started in late February, saw energy prices spike around the world.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three "non-compliant" oil tankers caught fire while going through the Strait. Tehran has regularly attacked vessels going through the Strait of Hormuz without its approval.
Aramco building hit after rocket attack
Elsewhere in the Middle East, the escalation between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia continued to rage.
Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted incoming missiles shot in the direction of the capital, Riyadh, on Sunday.
Debris from the interception damaged a building belonging to state-owned oil company Aramco. No casualties were reported, but some of the building's floors were heavily damaged, witnesses told AP.
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen-based militant group Houthisof launching two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles.
While Houthis carried out such attacks in the past, the rebels have not claimed responsibility for the attack yet.
According to the Houthis, 33 people were killed in Saudi-led attacks on Yemen's rebel-held capital, Sanaa, on Saturday.

articles.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
articles.summary: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives African philosophies including exploring how…

blocks.text: African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The author, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, who abandoned English to write in Gikuyu – a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya. Photograph: Mark Boster/LA Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

articles.title: Polish prosecutors open terrorism investigation into Kraków shooting
articles.summary: Officials say suspect holds far-right views and three people found dead at his home were his parents and sister Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation after a 24-year-old man opened…

blocks.text: Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation after a 24-year-old man opened fire in a busy market square in Kraków, killing six people including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that authorities said was probably inspired by far-right ideologies.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack on Saturday afternoon were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its western European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

The Kraków suspect, a Polish national, drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect, who was apprehended and taken to hospital after being wounded in an exchange of fire with police, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

blocks.caption: People mourn on Sunday near the scene of the shooting. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters

blocks.text: Four women and two men were killed, including a British citizen, Polish police said. Three of the victims were Polish women and the remaining two have not yet been identified. Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom is in a serious condition. The suspect underwent surgery in hospital, where he is under heavy police guard.

The bodies of the suspect’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Mourners have left candles in tribute to victims in the square, which was still partially cordoned off on Sunday. Flags across the country have been lowered to half mast, as have European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

The Polish defense minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, called the shooting an “act of terror” on the people of Kraków, Poland’s second largest city, which receives 15 million visitors a year, most of them passing through the main square.

blocks.caption: A woman places a candle among tributes near the scene. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters

blocks.text: Kraków authorities said the square and adjoining streets “as well as sections along the perpetrator’s escape route will be closed for several hours”. Police in Warsaw, the Polish capital, said security had been bolstered there.

Maria, a 20-year-old employee at a cafe in Warsaw, told Reuters she “almost burst into tears” when she heard about the attack in Kraków. “Recent events – not just this one, but things happening lately – are really affecting our sense of security,” ⁠she said.
The daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita said in an editorial that the mass shooting had brought a “brutal end ​to an era in which Poland was ​considered an island of safety”.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “I’m shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today,. My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said his country stood in solidarity with its neighbour, calling the shooting a shocking crime.

France’s Emmanuel Macron described “shock and disbelief following the tragic shooting in Kraków”, while the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said: “The events in Kraków have deeply affected me,” adding that Germany stood with Poland “as a friend and partner in these difficult times”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, expressed condolences to Poland “following the vile and unacceptable act of violence”.

articles.title: HOMESTRETCH: Surfing legends make history in Siargao
articles.summary: From a little-known island to a global stage, Cloud 9’s world-class waves capture the charm of Filipino culture and talent

blocks.text: From a little-known island to a global stage, Cloud 9’s world-class waves capture the charm of Filipino culture and talent
SURIGAO DEL NORTE, Philippines – The top 40 surfers in the world made Siargao a global stage.

As the Philippines hosted the 11th stop of the World Surf League’s 2026 Championship Tour for the first time, the best international surfers got a chance to experience the world-class waves of Cloud 9 in Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte from October 31 to November 3.
Rounding out the 40 participants were the top four Filipino surfers who competed as wildcard entries for the Philippines Pro:

items: 15-year-old Mara Lopez, who was born and raised in La Union
22-year-old French-Filipino Noah Arkfeld from Siargao
21-year-old and Siargao native Jayuard Alciso, who won bronze in the shortboard category of the 2026 Asian Games
30-year-old and top Filipino surfer John Mark ‘Marama’ Tokong

blocks.text: The Filipinos defied expectations, with Alciso and Tokong reaching Round 2 of the competition.
Brazil’s Gabriel Medina and United States’ Caitlyn Simmers claimed the top honors in the men’s and women’s category, respectively.

In this episode, HOMESTRETCH host Pató Gregorio speaks with the country’s bets — the four Filipinos who proved that they’re among the sport’s exciting discoveries, growing up in these previously little-known islands and eventually taking on the biggest names in world surfing.

Gregorio also chats with World Surf League Asia and Pacific president Andrew Stark on how the Philippines Pro came to be, sharing their thoughts on the Philippine surfing community, and what the country’s hosting means for the sport.
HOMESTRETCH tells stories of people whose struggles and triumphs inspire others, along with the places that help define the Filipino spirit.
Watch on Sunday, November 8, 8 pm, on Rappler’s YouTube channel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?
articles.summary: Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are…

blocks.text: As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.
What is Cop31?

From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks. This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.

While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.
How will co-convening work?

Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.

blocks.caption: The Paris climate agreement was adopted in 2015, committing countries to pursue efforts to limit global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. Photograph: François Mori/AP

blocks.text: Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane, improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy.
What are likely to be the key issues?

The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached, but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

blocks.caption: A survivor in a house damaged by flash floods in Nepal. Developing countries are calling for more financial support to cope with severe climate-related disasters. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP

blocks.text: Developing countries are also in dire need of help to cope with the hastening impacts of the climate crisis. After the disaster in Nepal, the country has been granted access to the global fund for “loss and damage” – the rescue and rehabilitation of communities stricken by climate-related disasters. But it is not enough, and poor countries also lack the means to adapt their infrastructure to worsening extreme weather.
Rich countries have been cutting their overseas aid, while rising interest rates have loaded further debt on to the poor.
What about fossil fuels?

It was not until 2023 at Cop28 that the final agreement directly addressed fossil fuels for the first time, due to long-term strident opposition from producing countries. The agreement included a resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels” but no deadline or plan for doing so. It is still tricky to get fossil fuels directly on to the Cop agenda, which requires consensus from nearly all parties, but this year the issue will be addressed through a non-binding “roadmap” for the global transition away from fossil fuels.
What would success look like?

Given the tense and fragile geopolitical situation – some commentators believe we are already in the midst of an unacknowledged third world war, while inflation and a rising far right are upsetting economies – countries might be tempted to settle for a quiet meeting.

blocks.caption: Activists participate in a demonstration to end the use of fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.  Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: But there are hopes for a better outcome, which could include: acceptance of the plans Brazil has produced and a promise to carry them forward; progress on climate finance for developing countries; a resolution to the row over climate science that has plagued recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; and the fleshing out of the “just transition mechanism” designed to help workers reliant on fossil fuels to adjust to a low-carbon economy.

Progress is also possible through Cop-related means outside the formal negotiations. Earlier this year, more than 60 countries, including the UK, the EU and dozens of developing nations, gathered in Colombia to vow to “transition away from fossil fuels”. This “coalition of the willing” could be boosted at Cop31 by new members, as well as fresh impetus from the recent success of political movements in several countries – Brazil, Canada, Serbia, Hungary and the US in states that decisively rejected Donald Trump at the midterms.
What can be achieved without the US?

Several prominent members of the US Congress may attend, along with businesspeople and US civil society groups, so there will be representation beyond the White House’s absence. Trump appears intent on boosting fossil fuel interests as much as possible in the US, but with oil prices still high after his war in Iran, the economics of low-carbon energy look ever more favourable.
Are there any reasons to be cheerful?

The geopolitics and the technology. Although the winds of conflict have upended international relations, they have also shown countries can benefit from the energy security that results from decentralised renewable generation. China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles, and its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal. This is saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars.

blocks.caption: The recent re-election of Lula in Brazil has cheered climate supporters. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters

blocks.text: Solar is booming in Africa at last, while in Pakistan a consumer-led rooftop revolution now produces about a quarter of the electricity used. Close to half of new cars in countries from Vietnam to some EU members are now electric.

Electrification will be a key focus of Cop31, and the high efficiency of electric technology means it could reduce the amount of primary energy use by half across the world, according to University of Oxford professor Jan Rosenow.

Politically, the re-election of Lula as president in Brazil has also cheered climate supporters. Lula will attend Cop, his first international visit since re-election, and is likely to be a fiery presence, showing progressive parties around the world how to win while championing the climate.

articles.title: Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks
articles.summary: What are the relationships and dominant interests in play, as the summit kicks off after a bitter row over its hosting? Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese…

blocks.text: Australia

Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid, and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers, and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.

blocks.caption: Chris Bowen in the House of Representatives in Canberra. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.
Turkey
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental issues before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.

In the last five years Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.

blocks.caption: Emine Erdoğan has called for an end to ‘throwaway culture’. Photograph: Ahmet Serdar Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to the “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.

Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.
Brazil

The recently re-elected President Lula da Silva will come to Cop31 for his first trip abroad after winning his historic fourth term, and will bring two roadmaps, one a global plan for the transition away from fossil fuels, the other for halting and reversing deforestation. These are non-binding, and contain no deadlines or firm requirements from governments, but show a series of steps that governments can take to achieve these key goals.
China

Xi Jinping, the president of China, will not come to this year’s Cop, but his country’s rapid energy and industrial transformation will determine the course of the planet’s future. China is the world’s second biggest economy and the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, making up nearly a third of global annual carbon output, due mainly to a huge use of fossil fuels to power its explosive economic growth for the last 25 years. But it also invested in renewable energy, which is reshaping the global energy business.

Xi may not be present in Antalya, but the top officials he sends will know that petrostates – including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are his important allies. However, countries pushing for a low-carbon future may be more important still – as China’s customers.
India

For several months this year, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, mulled an intriguing proposition: to host the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028. In the end, India withdrew its bid in April without specifying why, leaving the field open. India is torn between its burgeoning clean energy sector – it now has the world’s third biggest installed capacity of renewable energy, after China and the US – and its coal sector, which still supplies about 70% of electricity, and has close links to Modi. Bhupender Yadav, India’s environment minister, who leads its Cop delegations, enjoys a mutually supportive relationship with the UK’s Ed Miliband, and a reputation as a forward thinker.
US

The attention of Donald Trump has been fixed on the crucial midterm elections, a verdict on his second term as president that has shown Republicans the electoral dangers of an unpredictable White House. No US delegation is expected at Cop31, and soon Trump’s withdrawal of the country from the UN framework convention on climate change will mean none can take part.

Trump’s shadow was felt at Cop30 in Belem last year, as he started to dismantle the US’s renewable energy sector and boost fossil fuels, setting the US on course to start increasing greenhouse gas emissions again, after decades in which they fell. But his administration’s unpopularity with the US electorate, and a drought and fire-filled summer, has bolstered the pro-climate stance of scores of Democratic congresspeople and state governors, despite a campaign of “climate hushing” before the midterms. Some of them, and a scattering of business leaders, may attend Cop31.
UK

Andy Burnham will attend Cop for the first time this year, after a mixed record on the climate since taking office. During the record-breaking heatwaves and droughts of this summer, the British prime minister was criticised for failing to speak out on the climate crisis. He subsequently made strong interventions affirming his support for the UK’s target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, but then backed the Jackdaw gasfield. No decision has been announced on the Rosebank oilfield yet.
after newsletter promotion

From December, Burnham will have a much bigger opportunity to craft climate policy on the international stage: the UK will take over the revolving presidency of the influential G20 group, which comprises the world’s biggest developed and developing economies. The Guardian understands that the UK will emphasise building resilience against the impacts of the climate crisis as a key focus of the G20 for its year-long presidency.

Miliband, now foreign secretary, and a veteran of many Cops both in government and opposition, is expected to accompany the prime minister to the leaders’ summit segment of Cop31. Miliband was hailed, in public and private, by many participants last year for his patient bridge-building that helped Brazil to rescue a deal from the fractious final hours of Cop30.

At this year’s UN general assembly, he also briefed other governments on the findings of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, which warned that the impact of collapsing ecosystems around the world posed a national security risk, threatening food shortages, mass migration and potential nuclear war.
The energy and net zero secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, will head the UK’s Cop31 delegation for the final negotiations in the last days of this fortnight of talks, after the leaders have departed.
Europe

The EU has faced a quandary over its climate convictions in recent years. Far-right populists are on the rise, pushing climate denialism, and the bloc has backed down from some key regulations, watering down its green deal package, loosening the strings on corporate climate liabilities, delaying rules on trade in goods from deforested areas, and extending the phase-in of new car rules. The failure of Europe’s car industry to move decisively to electric vehicles – preferring lobbying against emissions standards, which has turned out to be a poor strategy as consumers turn in droves to cheap-to-run EVs – has led to threats to slap tariffs on China.

Despite calling this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves and drought a “summer of truth” that must be answered, the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is not confirmed for Cop31. Wopke Hoekstra, the Dutch climate commissioner, will oversee the final stages of the talks for the EU, and is likely to make competition with China a key focus.
UN

Cop31 will mark the final outing at a UN climate summit for António Guterres, the UN secretary general, who has regularly intervened powerfully on this subject. A successor to Guterres has still not yet been chosen – the US has tried to get Viktor Orbán, the far-right former president of Hungary, into the role, or a former minister from the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh.

blocks.caption: Simon Stiell oversees the talks. Photograph: Bernd Arnold/The Guardian

blocks.text: Simon Stiell, the determined and serious executive secretary of the UNFCCC, will oversee the talks, with an added twist to his job this year from having to liaise between the two co-hosts as well as the fractious parties.
Saudi

Saudi failed to confirm with the Guardian before Cop who would lead its delegation, but the country’s recent behaviour at international climate meetings tells its own story. Saudi has a long history of obstructing the UN climate negotiations, though its behaviour was sometimes muted when the US intervened. With Trump in the White House, Saudi has felt emboldened to interfere further, with allies including Russia, Venezuela, members of the Arab group, and the Like-Minded Developing Countries grouping.

At Cop30, the Saudi delegation refused to allow even an oblique mention of the pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, made at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, into the final text until the final moments.

At recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Saudi led a small group of countries – including China, India, Russia and Kenya – that fought to delay publication of the next comprehensive assessment of climate science. Publication of the landmark report, which is expected to warn of catastrophic impacts from further temperature rises, was expected in 2028, in time for Cop33 at which countries will assess their progress on meeting emissions-cutting goals under the Paris agreement, a process known as the “global stocktake”. Delaying it by a year or more, as Saudi wants, would mean a loss of urgency for the global stocktake, and could help countries to get away with inadequate measures on decarbonisation.

articles.title: Regina councillor shared great replacement conspiracy theory with colleagues during mosque broadcast debate
articles.summary: Emails obtained by CBC News show internal city discussions about a Regina mosque's decision to broadcast the adhan, or Islamic call to prayer.

image.caption: Ward 1 Coun. Dan Rashovich writes on a note pad during an executive committee meeting on Dec. 4, 2024. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

blocks.text: As Regina debated a mosque's decision to broadcast a call to prayer, Ward 1 Coun. Dan Rashovich forwarded an email to his colleagues that contained what experts say is the "great replacement" conspiracy theory, which falsely suggests immigrants are attempting to replace a country's white population.
The email, obtained by CBC News through a freedom of information request, says the Islamic call to prayer or adhan is a "strategic tactic" to expand Islam in Canada through changing demographics.

"Thank You for your email. You nailed it!" Rashovich wrote in an email CC'd to every member of Regina city council, as well as Regina police Chief Lorilee Davies, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and provincial Justice Minister Tim McLeod.
Rashovich declined multiple requests for an on-camera interview. Instead, in a series of emailed statements, Rashovich said he did not not see the email's entire contents before sharing it.

items: Downtown Regina mosque resumes broadcasting call to prayer after threats

blocks.text: The city councillor said his "You nailed it!" response was referring to a different email from the same sender — an email that doesn't refer to the great replacement conspiracy theory. That email was redacted when provided to CBC.
But one of Rashovich's colleagues did not interpret Rashovich's comment as reacting to a different email.
Ward 6 Coun. Victoria Flores pushed back on the email containing the Islamophobic screed, saying the City of Regina needed to call the email "exactly what it is."
"This unnamed person is explicitly calling for violence and the destruction of places of worship in our city," Flores wrote.
Rashovich told CBC he could not comment on the "accuracy of religious interpretations," and that he did not respond or agree with the email that contains the passage with the conspiracy theory in it.

Amin Asfari, a professor and researcher at the University of Regina, says the email promotes fears that Europeans or Canadians with European heritage are being replaced through a so-called "white genocide."
Regina mosque halts broadcasting call to prayer after backlash

Jasmin Zine, a professor of sociology and religion at Wilfred Laurier University who has studied Islamophobia, says the conspiracy theory is prominent among white supremacists, nationalists and neo-nazis.
This example, which hinges on Islamophobia, preys on fears of replacement.
"It assumes there's kind of a nefarious intention by people who are immigrants," Asfari said.
'A glaring hypocrisy': professor
Rashovich made his own views on the broadcast of the adhan clear in an email dated July 6, 2026.
The email shows Rashovich responding to an email that is entirely redacted. Rashovich's response is CC'd to the rest of council.
"I agree this should not be happening," Rashovich said, saying he believes in freedom of worship but not at the "expense of publicly expressing this on everybody."
Rashovich says the country was founded on "Judeo Christian values" and that "Religion and Politics should not mix."
"Every religion has the right to worship who and how they want and this should be done within their church besides some outdoor events or marches that happen," Rashovich said.

items: Regina mosque surveys public after backlash to broadcast of call to prayer

blocks.text: He goes on to say that the city's noise bylaw allows the broadcast of the adhan "when it should not be allowed."
"We do not need others religious messages being broadcasted. That is for every Religion," Rashovich wrote.
When asked whether he stands by this email, Rashovich said that it must be read in context.
Asfari said the email is an example of hypocrisy from Rashovich.

The University of Regina professor said the email shows Rashovich acknowledging that religious freedom is a central concept to the Canadian identity, while also stating that certain aspects of faith should be relegated away from the general public.
Asfari said religions often use a call to prayer. In Christianity there is the ringing of church bells, in Judaism the shofar horn is used and Islam uses the adhan.

"There's a glaring hypocrisy, and it comes across rather consistently, when people like this speak about what they believe to be the kind of supreme or dominant narrative that must be there, and then the other, which is foreign, must be tucked away," Asfari said.
The email
Rashovich's email that CC's the Islamophic conspiracy theory was sent on the evening of July 14, 2026. CBC obtained it through a freedom of information request filed with the City of Regina.
At that time, the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque had recently paused its plans to broadcast the adhan over the noon hour on Fridays.
The mosque had obtained a permit from the Regina Police Service allowing it to broadcast the three-minute call over rooftop speakers once a week, under the city's noise bylaw.
M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid, told media that he later decided to pause broadcasts because the mosque had received threats after the first broadcast.
M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque in downtown Regina, poses for a photo outside of the centre on July 17. (Randi LaRocque/CBC)
The email containing the Islamophic message — including who sent it — is redacted in the emails disclosed by the city, but it is partially quoted by Flores in a later email.
The message says the adhan directs adherents to spread the religion in "non-Muslim lands" through "public assertion" and "demographic presence," according to Flores' quotation.

Zine said the message references the great replacement conspiracy theory and the civilizational jihad conspiracy theory, which falsely claims that Muslims immigrants are attempting to establish social, cultural and political strongholds in nations that they are "infiltrating."
The tying of two different conspiracy theories together in one message paints a picture of a grand Islamophobic plan, he said.

"The idea is that Muslims are a Trojan horse that will unleash these invaders who will infiltrate Western societies. They will install themselves politically as a fifth column and then start installing Sharia law," Zine said.
Asfari said Islamophobic conspiracy theories can be precursor to violence, saying it "does tend to plant seeds in more nefarious circles where the propensity for violence is greater."
Zine and Asfari point to the 2017 Quebec City mosque shooting and the 2021 London truck attack as examples of rhetoric becoming action in Canada.
Londoners honour the Afzaal family on the anniversary of their tragic deaths
Asfari and Zine said it's particularly concerning that a municipal politician — rather than a random person online — is sharing the conspiracy theory.

Zine said municipal leaders and politicians are looked to as trusted sources of information. When they share conspiracy theories that are otherwise circulating in white nationalist echo chambers, it helps to legitimize beliefs that are otherwise clearly false and harmful.
"It does give average people more licence to share those stories. And maybe they believe that those are bona fide," Zine said.
A person within an institution, or an institution itself, sharing a conspiracy theory can help give it more weight, Asfari said.
"When we talk about institutionalized Islamophobia, this is precisely the kind of thing that we're talking about," Asfari said.
Asfari commended other councillors for pushing back against the rhetoric in the email.
In one example, Flores directly confronts Rashovich for sharing it.
"...Differentiate between a noise bylaw concern and someone who is using this opportunity to spread misinformation and hate," Flores wrote.

articles.title: Gaza: Rains add misery to humanitarian catastrophe
articles.summary: With most homes damaged or destroyed by the war, Gazans are facing worsening humanitarian conditions due to heavy rain.

image.caption: Gaza's displaced people saw heavy rains that soaked tents and mattressesImage: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP

blocks.text: Heavy rains sweeping across parts of the Middle East this week have flooded tens of thousands of tents in Gaza's displaced persons' camps.
According to authorities in the enclave, at least 70,000 tents have been flooded over the past day, where tens of thousands of people took shelter.
No fatalities had been reported, although some people were injured.
Some of the tents have been washed away due to the weather, with mattresses and blankets soaked with water.

blocks.caption: Around 1 million Palestinians live in camps that lack proper shelter, water and sanitationImage: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS

blocks.text: Majority of houses destroyed
More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

UN data says some 80% of the enclave's structures have been damaged during the war, with two-thirds destroyed, leaving Gaza's residents — many of whom were displaced multiple times during the war between Israel and Hamas — to either live in tents or risk their lives and seek shelter in buildings that could be on the verge of collapse.
The Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine released a statement appealing for humanitarian aid for the Gaza Strip due to the situation.

blocks.caption: Tents were flooded as a result of the heavy rains in the regionImage: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to the committee, some 950,000 people are living in areas "vulnerable to flooding," with more than 400,000 living in areas of "high levels of risk."

"Heavy rainfall is compounding an already catastrophic humanitarian situation, leaving displaced families and those who have lost their homes exposed to the elements and deprived of the most basic necessities of life," the statement said.
Israel accused of genocide

Some 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip since October 7, 2023. The war was triggered when Islamist Palestinian organization Hamas and its affiliates launched a terrorist attack in Israel's south, killing some 1,200 Israelis, most of whom were civilians. The militants also kidnapped 251 hostages.
The UN, EU, US and Israel, among others, consider Hamas to be a terrorist organization.

A UN commission of inquiry, as well as many leading human rights organizations, have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. Israel has rejected the accusation, saying its army is acting in accordance with international law.

articles.title: Alex Eala suffers season-ending stunner as Liu dominates Hong Kong final
articles.summary: Alex Eala absorbs a stunning shutout loss against American underdog Claire Liu at the Hong Kong Open finale, bringing a heartbreaking end to her 2026 season

blocks.text: FOCUSED. Filipino tennis star Alex Eala gets ready to return a shot during the 2026 Hong Kong Open.
HONG KONG OPEN
Alex Eala absorbs a stunning shutout loss against American underdog Claire Liu at the Hong Kong Open finale, bringing a heartbreaking end to her 2026 season

items: Filipina tennis player Alex Eala faced a disappointing defeat against American Claire Liu in the final of the Hong Kong Open, losing 6-3, 6-0.
Liu's victory marked her first career singles title at the WTA 250 level, following her previous wins at WTA 125 championships.
Despite the loss, Eala reflected positively on her successful 2026 season, which included reaching the Hong Kong Open final and winning the WTA 500 Washington DC Open.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala met a disappointing end to what was otherwise a prolific Hong Kong Open run, and a historic 2026 season overall, as American foe Claire Liu cruised to a dominant 6-3, 6-0 title-winning finale on Sunday, November 8.
With the stunning win over the world No. 17 Eala, world No. 102 Liu finally earned a breakthrough career singles title at the WTA 250 level after earning two WTA 125 championships.

Liu’s title win marked a second consecutive upset at the Filipina icon’s expense, as the 26-year-old, then world No. 305, booted the top-50 Eala at the 2025 Guangzhou Open first round in their only other head-to-head meeting.
With that footnote likely in the back of their minds, Liu kept her aggression up from the get-go, seizing the opening frame with a 3-0 finish from a competitive 3-3 deadlock to set the tone, 6-3.

Desperate to turn the tide, Eala poured everything she had into the first game of the second set, denying four break points in a prolonged back-and-forth point trade before finally losing her serve and the first point to Liu.

Likely out of gas and definitely out of momentum, Eala faded quicker as the points piled on, losing her serve in the third and fifth games before Liu finally put the Filipina out of her misery with a stunning bagel finish, 6-0, and nine straight won games for the title.

The 6-0 burial marked a dim end to a monumental 2026 season for Eala, who proved worthy of her lofty world ranking with a sensational rise to the Hong Kong Open final and a career milestone WTA 500 Washington DC Open championship last August.

“First and foremost, I want to congratulate Claire on an amazing tournament, a great week and a great match. Very, very well deserved congratulations. I’d like to thank the tournament staff and the organizers for the amazing hospitality, the physios for keeping me together,” Eala said.

“And of course, the fans, thank you, thank you, thank you. I mean, wrapping up this year, you guys do not know how much meaning you add on top of what I do, and how much of a pleasure it is to go about my life sharing these moments with you all. So I’m forever grateful.”

Eala soon heads home to bask in her career highs and 2026 season overall with a big homecoming event, “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate,” at the massive Philippine Arena on December 8. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tesla to pull the plug on Cybertruck after years of poor sales
articles.summary: Tesla will add an extra production shift to try to complete outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the line next year for a planned expansion of Cybercab production

blocks.text: CYBERTRUCK. A Tesla Cybertruck sits in the parking lot of a Tesla facility in the Queens borough of New York City, U.S., September 16, 2026.
Shannon Stapleton/Reuters
Tesla will add an extra production shift to try to complete outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the line next year for a planned expansion of Cybercab production

items: Tesla will cease Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027 due to weak sales, allowing a shift in focus to the Cybercab, a key part of Tesla's autonomous vehicle strategy.
The Cybertruck has faced significant challenges, including design criticisms, regulatory hurdles in Europe, and disappointing sales figures, leading to multiple recalls since its launch in late 2023.

Musk's pivot towards the Cybercab reflects a broader strategy to transition Tesla from a traditional automaker to a robotics and AI company, despite the Cybercab's production still being in its early stages.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, November 6, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk’s pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker’s autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday’s US midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.
Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion in market capitalization for the week.

Tesla will add an extra production shift to try to complete outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the line next year for a planned expansion of Cybercab production, CEO Elon Musk said Saturday.
“The Cybertruck order backlog is currently far more than Tesla can make before dismantling the line for Cybercab expansion around June/July next year,” Musk said in a post on X.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era.”
Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The US EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
“It doesn’t make sense to keep it going when it’s not meeting its targets,” said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. “Every rational auto guy would say the same.”
“It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla’s balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves.”
Musk’s SpaceX was one of the model’s biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.
The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.
During Cybertruck’s official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying “finally, the future will look like the future.”

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.
Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.
“All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren’t popular in the US,” Munoz said.

But Cybertruck’s sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.
“Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won’t go, can’t go,” former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.
The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk’s key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.
Musk has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk’s self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency’s questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification.
“Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon. The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year. Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units.
About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The struggle with declaring #WalangPasok
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s new executive order seems to be an EO that Malacañang itself badly needs, after a string of blanket class suspensions

blocks.text: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s new executive order seems to be an EO that Malacañang itself badly needs, after a string of blanket class suspensions

“Talaga lang ha?” was my initial, no-filter reaction when Malacañang announced that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had signed an executive order (EO) establishing a framework for class suspensions and resumptions.

EO No. 130 explicitly allows for area- and school-level decisions to be made on when to suspend or resume classes — a targeted approach as opposed to blanket orders covering entire provinces or even regions.

Hello, I’m Acor Arceo, head of news operations at Rappler. I also oversee our coverage of the education sector and disasters, among others, which explains why I was probably the most skeptical in our newsroom when Marcos’ new EO was publicly released on Tuesday, November 3.

When I instructed our education reporter Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring to write an article on the EO, I also pointed out that Malacañang had often been the one to step in and declare blanket class suspensions — in trigger-happy fashion, really.
It was like the Palace gave itself the order it badly needed.

Let’s backtrack a bit to 2025. Remember when Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla drew flak for his flippant way of announcing class suspensions? The approach that made him a social media star as Cavite governor had the opposite effect when he took it to the national stage. At the time, the focus was on Remulla’s choice of words and overall tone, which lacked the formality befitting his position and the gravity of the situation.
There were also instances when Remulla’s announcements somehow excluded one or more affected provinces, raising even more questions about whether or not he was making well-informed decisions.

Thankfully, the poorly worded social media announcements from the Department of the Interior and Local Government eventually stopped. What didn’t stop back then, however, was Malacañang’s blanket class suspension policy.

Up until last September, the Palace was still suspending face-to-face classes for entire areas, seemingly disregarding the fact that these areas were facing different weather conditions and varying risk levels. Sure, there was a line in each Malacañang memorandum acknowledging the authority of local chief executives to decide for their respective cities, municipalities, or provinces, but who would deviate from an order that already came from the top?

In one instance, the Palace suspension order came late afternoon, when school and work hours were almost over. People could only shake their heads and wonder: a) Is this supposed to be for tomorrow? b) Is Malacañang in a different timezone? c) Is this even for real?

The executive branch also seemed to have forgotten that every school day counts in a country facing a severe learning crisis. This is not to say that we should make students go to class at all costs, without care for their safety. It’s about ensuring that those who can safely attend classes are actually able to do so, instead of them automatically being lumped together with students in areas facing harsh conditions.
Implementing guidelines for Marcos’ new EO are expected to be released within 30 days. Join us in scrutinizing the guidelines once they’re out. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure
articles.summary: Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust…

image.caption: A mural at the Bonn exhibition shows people moments before being sent to the gas chambersImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

blocks.caption: Jens-Christian Wagner reports on rampant disrespect at the Buchenwald Memorial and warns against the distortion of historyImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner says that Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.
The new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.
Moralizing doesn't help people learn

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner says. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students. "Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit."

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explains. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

blocks.caption: Visiting a Holocaust memorial site is a required part of the curriculum at many schoolsImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner says, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example. "For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism."
Holocaust survivor: 'The number tattooed on my arm was always there'
Eva Umlauf knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition. Now, she's 83.

But in November 1944, she was just two years old when the Nazis deported her, her pregnant mother and her father from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using them as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.
Germany's darkest chapter: Auschwitz and the Holocaust

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Eva's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her. Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

blocks.caption: Eva Umlauf has been president of the International Auschwitz Committee since 2025Image: Alessandra Schellnegger/SZ Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eva Umlauf: 'I cannot forgive'
Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and Eva moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she says. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

blocks.caption: An interactive digital testimony has been created for the exhibition, for which Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf answered 1,000 questionsImage: Bright White Ltd.

blocks.text: It was not until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."
'Take care of your country'

Eva Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stresses. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. (…) You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color." She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."
The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Poland begins two days of mourning over Krakow shooting
articles.summary: Mourners left candles in Krakow's main market square to honor the victims of the attack. Police confirmed that the bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his parents and sister.

image.caption: Mourners lay candles in Krakow's main square to pay their respects Image: Jakub Porzycki/REUTERS

blocks.text: Poland began two days of mourning on Sunday, a day after killed six people and wounded 15 others were shot in Krakow's main market square.
The attack occurred in Main Square (Rynek Glowny) in the Old Town of Poland's second-largest city on Saturday. The area is a popular tourist attraction.
In addition to the six people killed in the square, three bodies found at the suspect's home were the bodies of his sister, mother and father, police said Sunday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labeled the attack an act of far-right "terrorism," but authorities have not given a possible motive.
Mourners left candles in the square to pay tribute to the victims of the shooting. Black flags and Polish flags with black ribbons were also seen in the city.
The square remained partially sealed off on Sunday morning as authorities continued investigations.

blocks.caption: The site of the shooting remained partially cordoned off on Sunday morningImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: What do we know about the shooting in Krakow's Main Square?
The 24-year-old suspect, who was wearing military fatigues at the time of the attack, allegedly shot at people at random as he drove around the square.
He was wounded by police and is in critical condition in hospital.
Polish authorities say the man held right-wing extremist and ultranationalist views.
"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said at a news conference.
A British national was among the dead, and among the wounded were citizens of Austria, the United Kingdom, Germany, Portugal and Russia, according to authorities.
Two police officers were wounded while confronting the suspect and are in hospital. Officials have launched an appeal for blood donations for one of the officers, who is in critical condition.
The Krakow Carriage Driver's Association told Polish news agency PAP that several horse-drawn carriage drivers were seriously injured in the shooting.
Police confirm three bodies found were members of suspect's family
Police said on Sunday that three bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his sister, mother and father.
The family home is in the town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.
Police said that several firearms were seized from the apartment.
The suspect had no previous criminal record, according to Polish media reports.
He and his father were members of a shooting club.

articles.title: How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
articles.summary: Video authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment gunshots rang out in Krakow's main market square.

blocks.text: Six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second largest city, on Saturday.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows about a dozen people running inside two buildings before a black car with its front window open passes, followed by a police car.
Another video shows the moment that gunshots were heard in the city's main market square.
Poland's interior minister described the suspect - a 25-year-old Polish citizen - as being inspired by "far-right ideologies"; police said he used "military weapons" in the attack.
Hours after the attack, Polish PM Donald Tusk said three other bodies were found at the suspect's home, which is still being searched.

articles.title: Analysis of crime-scene blood and bullets can be pivotal in court cases. But how reliable is it?
articles.summary: Ballistic and blood spatter analysis are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, according to…

image.caption: A Texas Ranger holds a shell casing discovered at the crime scene as he testifies in a murder trial in Stephenville, Texas, in February 2015. A new analysis points to 'significant methodological flaws' in the research that backs up ballistics as a discipline. (Tom Fox/Pool/The Dallas Morning News/Th

blocks.text: World

Ballistic and blood spatter analysis are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, according to new research — while lawyers and judges don’t challenge those conclusions enough.
Researcher questions extent of what forensic evidence reveals, says lawyers need to challenge experts in court

Forensic analysis has a reputation for being reliably accurate, an assumption that's been polished by many crime TV dramas where ballistics and blood-spatter teams uncover essential evidence to catch the perpetrator.
But that assumption has found its way into courtrooms, where the accuracy of forensic analysis is rarely questioned, according to new research.

Both ballistic and blood spatter analysis, which examine evidence from a crime scene, are grounded in science. But its practitioners regularly make conclusions in court that are far beyond what their own empirical evidence supports, says researcher Sara Gordon — while lawyers and judges don’t challenge those conclusions enough.

"They're admitted largely because they've always been admitted and people just sort of assume that they're reliable," says Gordon, an associate professor at Peter A. Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia.

items: How Toronto police gather clues from guns seized off city streets

blocks.text: Qualified and admissible expert testimony on forensic evidence can provide "significant assistance" in understanding specific information in a case, a fact sheet from the Department of Justice says. Canada’s courts have allowed it to be included in cases for decades.
Using Canadian cases, Gordon examined these forensic and investigative techniques that informed evidence regularly admitted in court.

Her analysis of firearms evidence points to "significant methodological flaws" in the research that backs up ballistics as a discipline that may "underestimate error rates." She concludes that experts often don’t give courts the full story and give "a false impression" of the accuracy of their speciality.
Evidence markers are placed beside shell casings on the street outside a cafe that was shot at in Surrey, B.C., in August 2025. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)
Bullet proof?

To connect a bullet or casing found at a crime scene to a caliber of gun, ballistics examiners will compare other bullets or casings shot from test guns and examine them under a microscope to look for similarities.
Eventually a forensic scientist may end up in a courtroom testifying that the evidence found at a crime scene is or isn’t a match, citing research from their field to back up their conclusions.

Gordon says examiners will often testify that the error rate of the ballistics field is somewhere between one and two per cent. But the studies she examined for her research reported an error rate as high as 50 per cent.
She also says there are no set standards for the minimum number of similarities needed to match bullets.
"It's largely a subjective analysis," she said.
Courts must start questioning reliability of some forensic evidence, researcher says

Her research, which follows similar audits of forensic evidence in the United States, cites a case in Ontario in 2021, where a firearms examiner conceded under cross-examination that her conclusion — that shell casings from a crime scene matched a handgun found in the accused's apartment — was subjective.

The examiner later added there was “no specific number of agreements required between two items for her to conclude that there was a match" and she formed her opinion because she believed a match was "within the limits of practical certainty."

items: A$AP Rocky's trial starts with clash over ballistics report

blocks.text: The issue came to a head in a Chicago courtroom in 2023, where a judge, moved by a lack of "objective forensic based reasons," banned the use of ballistics matching in a criminal case.

The judge then reviewed a dozen other cases that resulted in a wrongful conviction from flawed ballistics matching, labelling it a "wake-up call to courts operating as rubber stamps in blindly finding general acceptance" of this type of evidence.

Bullet fragments are displayed on a screen in a Utah courtroom on July 9, during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk. (Spenser Heaps/Pool/The Associated Press)
Drawing from such decisions, Gordon argues that some ballistic experts shouldn't be testifying in cases where the science doesn't give them the ability to draw conclusions.
One senior forensic scientist who regularly testifies in court says being transparent about a discipline's limitations is key.

Darryl Barr, who examines weapons and tools linked to crimes for Bulletproof Forensic Consulting, maintains there is "a scientific basis for firearms examinations" and plenty of empirical evidence that supports experts' determinations — but he concedes they could do better at making that clearer in court.
Barr says he's reassured by the fact that virtually every country in the world uses forensic analysis as part of its judicial process, and adds that any scrutiny of his discipline is welcomed.
"Science improves through scrutiny and forensic science is not any different, obviously," he said.

Investigators gather ballistic evidence at two separate crime scenes. Left, New York police photograph bullets on the sidewalk where Brian Thompson, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, was fatally shot on Dec. 4, 2024. Right, the copper jacket of a bullet found near the scene of a shooting close to the White House on May 24 this year. (AP Photo/Stefan Jeremiah / AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
The CSI effect
Part of a prosecution or defence counsel's role is to scrutinize each other’s evidence. But digging into the accuracy of the science of forensic evidence doesn’t happen often, says Gordon.

She thinks part of the reason is that society at large has come to think ballistics and blood spatter are as definitive as DNA evidence and can reveal crucial details in an investigation — in part due to crime shows like Law and Order and the many spin-offs of CSI.
For example — despite what a slick, sunglasses-wearing fictional detective might say — the science of blood spatter cannot indicate if a person was acting deliberately or not.
A physical comparison supervisor at the Vermont Forensic Laboratory examines a shell casing in March 2015. (Wilson Ring/The Associated Press)
Gordon's separate research on blood spatter analysis found the detail to which some experts testify is sometimes very specific, such as inferring what an accused's mental state might have been.

She points to a B.C. case from 2009 where the Crown used analysis of blood patterns in a crime scene to reconstruct the actions of the accused, arguing he had guilty intent because of the way blood was "projected" during the attack.

items: Investigators found presumed blood stains in garage years after alleged murder, court hears

blocks.text: "There are no studies testing or establishing an error rate for conclusions about an individual’s mental state based on bloodstain patterns," she writes in her research.
"There's just no indication, in the science, that we can make those sorts of conclusions," she told CBC News.
'Frailties of the evidence'
The danger of lawyers not challenging expert witness testimony in court is recognized in case law, says Rebecca McConchie, president of the Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia.
So, too, is the risk of judges and juries not appreciating the "frailties of the evidence when assessing it," she said in a statement to CBC News.
"It is so important for people to keep an open mind when they hear about criminal justice issues or evidence held out as obvious proof of a person’s guilt," McConchie said.
A statue of Themis, goddess of justice, at the B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver, pictured on Oct. 6. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
Ultimately, Gordon says, Canada has received far less attention in legal literature and she wants her studies to make the country's courts better at doing their job of determining guilt or innocence.

She says her work is about providing information about the evidence behind the evidence for lawyers and judges to be able to ask more questions — to "lay that out for them in a way that just makes them view the evidence a little bit more skeptically."

items: Jury hears forensic expert detail evidence in 30-year cold case sex assault trial

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the RCMP, which provides forensic services across Canada, said it was aware of the research and that it's still committed to using established scientific methodologies, quality assurance processes and professional standards in its work.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Georgie Smyth is a CBC Network Reporter and Producer in Vancouver. She's worked for BBC World News in London and for Nine News in Australia. She's focused on local, national and international stories that affect all Canadians. Got an idea or story tip? Email: georgina.smyth@cbc.ca
